C01.caveat: The ICDD card itself was not opened because the database is closed. The identity rests on papers that quote the card, all consistent with each other: at least 7 papers from different groups in China, Korea, Colombia and Saudi Arabia/Italy. Two of them state P42/mnm explicitly with the card (Wang et al. 2020 JMCA; Liu & Zhang 2020 RSC Adv), and one adds "(136)" (Zhu et al. 2026 Adv Mater). No conflicting attribution was found: all 24 open-access Europe PMC full texts citing 40-1290 attach it to RuO2. Some of them name only "RuO2" without giving the phase. RuO2 does have non-rutile polymorphs: the CaCl2-type Pnnm (COD 2101931) and the high-pressure Pa-3 (COD 1540048). No source attaches 40-1290 to either of them. The card's own lattice parameters (search snippets gave a = 4.4994, c = 3.1071 Å) come only from search-engine summaries and were not confirmed from an opened source, so they are not relied on here. The OPTIMADE record for mp-825 has empty space-group fields; the space group comes from the MP legacy page and from COD. The Frontiers quote was extracted by the page-fetch tool, not read from a PDF.

C02.identity: ICDD/JCPDS PDF card 43-1019 (= 00-043-1019) is iridium dioxide, IrO2. It is the tetragonal rutile-type phase, space group P4_2/mnm (No. 136). The papers put the card cell at a = b = 4.4983 Å, c = 3.1544 Å. These match the peaks the review papers index to the card.

C02.caveat:
1. I could not open the ICDD card itself, because the database is not open. The identity rests on four papers from different groups that all attach 43-1019 to IrO2, with no paper found attaching it to another phase:
   - Liu & Zhang, Shenzhen Angel Group (RSC Adv 2020)
   - Deng et al., Beijing Institute of Smart Energy / State Grid (Springer Proc. Phys. 2024)
   - Sun et al. (IET Nanobiotechnol 2026)
   - Luo et al. (Molecules 2025)
   Two of these papers state P42/mnm explicitly and one says 'rutile-phase'. The space group comes independently from COD 2101854 and 1548817 and from MP mp-2723 (via spglib).

2. One paper is internally inconsistent. In the same paragraph, Luo et al. (Molecules 2025, doi 10.3390/molecules30092069) also label graphite peaks '(002), (100), (101), (102), and (004) of the graphite (PDF#00-043-1019)' at 26.66–54.73°. Those are graphite positions, not IrO2 reflections, and the same authors assign the card to IrO2 a few sentences earlier. This looks like a copy-paste error inside one paper, not a real conflict between sources, so I kept rutile_type 'yes'. The reconciler should know about it.

3. The card cell given by Deng et al. (a = 4.4983, c = 3.1544 Å) differs slightly from COD 2101854 (4.5051 / 3.1586 Å). This is expected, since these are different measurements of the same phase.

4. The (111) peak at 40.17° lies very close to (200) at 39.99°. Papers that index '(111), (200)' are therefore still consistent with rutile IrO2.

5. A card match shows the reference pattern, not that a given sample is phase-pure. Amorphous IrOx or metallic Ir in a sample would need separate checking.

C04.caveat: The ICDD card itself is not openly accessible, so it was not opened. Its identity rests on four independent papers from different groups (Poitiers, Solapur, Hong Kong, South Africa). All four attach 88-0322 to tetragonal or rutile-type RuO2, and I found no paper assigning it to another phase. The space group comes from the databases for tetragonal RuO2 (COD 1000058, MP mp-825), not from the card. RuO2 has other polymorphs: an orthorhombic CaCl2-type Pnnm form (COD 2101931) and a cubic Pa-3 high-pressure form (COD 1540048). Neither is tetragonal, so a card described as tetragonal RuO2 can only be the rutile form. The lattice constants quoted in the papers (a≈4.49-4.51 Å, c≈3.05-3.11 Å) match the rutile cell. Two further points. First, Mfengwana & Sone (Sci Rep 2023) attach the card to reflections at 33.18°, 43.32° and 63.3° 2θ with indices (101), (210), (211). These do not match the standard rutile RuO2 lines the other papers cite (about 28.1° (110), 35.1° (101), 54.3° (211)). That is a problem with how that paper read its own pattern; it does not dispute what the card denotes. Second, the Materials Project OPTIMADE endpoint returned null space-group fields, so the space group for mp-825 comes from the legacy MP page.

C06.caveat:
1. The sources conflict, so under v5 D9 the result is "unresolved". Three uses of 88-0233 / 01-088-0233 name three different phases:
- RuO2: the Li 2026 preprint, S30868, the paper under review.
- fcc Ru: Yang et al. 2024, Chin. J. Catal.
- (Zr6.86Mg0.14)O11.28N1.72: HighScore reference panels in Bekmuldin 2025 and Skakov et al. 2024. This is one figure from one group, so it is a single source, not two independent ones.

2. The Zr-Mg oxynitride label is the only attribution that shows the card's own pattern, so it is the most credible. Its sticks (strongest near 30.1 deg, d ≈ 2.97 Å; others near 35, 50 and 59.6 deg) look like a fluorite-derived zirconia pattern. They contain no rutile RuO2 lines computed from COD 1000058: (110) 28.04 deg and (211) 54.31 deg. They also do not fit the fcc Ru d-spacings (2.2 / 1.9 Å) that Yang et al. report.

3. Both Ru uses are plausibly transcription errors of widely used cards: 88-0322 for tetragonal RuO2 and 88-2333 for fcc Ru. Checker 2 opened papers using those cards. I did not re-open them, and no source states that either use is a typo.

4. Two further checks on the preprint:
- It assigns a 0.31 nm fringe to RuO2 (111). Rutile (111) is about 0.222 nm, and 0.318 nm is (110), so the preprint is internally inconsistent.
- The card number therefore cannot establish rutile identity for S30868. Rutile status must come from the paper's own indexed peaks, compared with COD 1000058 (P4_2/mnm).

5. Gaps:
- No open database entry (COD or Materials Project) gives the Zr-Mg oxynitride. Its space group stays unknown, and the ICDD card itself was not read.
- The two-paper standard is not met for any single identity.
- WebSearch was unavailable (budget exhausted).

C07.caveat:
1. The ICDD card itself was not opened because it is proprietary. The identity rests on four independent documents from different groups that attach 73-1469 / 01-073-1469 to RuO2: a PNNL report (USA), a CNEA/CONICET paper (Argentina), a UFRN thesis (Brazil) and a UAM thesis (Spain). Two of them (the PNNL database legend and the UFRN thesis) state "Tetragonal" explicitly. The CNEA paper places it in a "rutile" context. No source attached the card to any other phase.
2. Three of the four sources are grey literature: one technical report and two theses. Only the Procedia Materials Science paper is a journal article. Four more hits appear in journal articles but were not opened: InfoMat 2022 (10.1002/inf2.12326), Small 2023 (10.1002/smll.202308841), a KAUST 2019 thesis, and the Inorg. Chem. 2025 La-doped RuO2 paper. Access was blocked (403 or bot block), so they are not used as evidence.
3. The "(C)" flag marks a calculated pattern, probably derived from ICSD. The PNNL legend line is cut off after "Tetragonal - a", so the card's exact cell and parent structure are not established from open sources. The space group is inferred, not read off the card: every tetragonal RuO2 entry in COD and Materials Project is P4_2/mnm (136). The other RuO2 polymorphs in COD are Pnnm (58, orthorhombic CaCl2-type, high pressure) and Pa-3 (205, cubic), neither of which is tetragonal.
4. Cross-check against the quoted planes: from the COD 1000058 cell (a = 4.4968, c = 3.1049 Å), Cu Kα reflections fall at (110) 28.04°, (101) 35.09°, (200) 40.07° and (211) 54.31° 2θ. These match the planes the papers quote.

C11.caveat:
1) The ICDD card was not viewed. The identity rests on six papers that cite 70-3132 for VO2. Three independent author groups name the polymorph, and all three say monoclinic: Ding et al. 2017 "VO2(M)", Yang et al. 2023 "monoclinic VO2" and Ma et al. 2022 "Monoclinic VO2". No paper found ties the card to rutile or tetragonal VO2. The exact space group is inferred: VO2(M1) is P2_1/c in COD 9009089 and 3000344. The rarer monoclinic M2 form is C2/m (COD 1521122). Neither is P4_2/mnm.
2) The quoting paper (Niu et al., Adv. Mater. 2024, Ru-VO2) names only "VO2 (PDF # 70-3132)" and gives no polymorph. Its peaks cannot tell monoclinic from rutile VO2. Simulated Cu Ka lines are 27.90/37.10/55.5 for M1 (COD 9009089) and 27.85/37.09/55.53 for rutile (COD 1539951). The paper's 27.21/36.57/54.81 sit about 0.6-0.7 degrees below both.
3) Its HR-TEM index "VO2 (-101)" uses a negative, monoclinic-style index. In standard P2_1/c, h0l reflections with odd l are extinct, so (-101) is not a standard M1 reflection. The index therefore implies a non-standard cell or a misindexing, and is not diagnostic.
4) The Rare Metals paper uses the same card for (100)/(200) peaks at 19.93/40.60 degrees and matches its Raman to a "Wadsley phase" of VO2. Those lines match neither simulated M1 nor rutile VO2. This shows loose use of the card by one group, but no rival polymorph assignment.
5) Monoclinic VO2(M1) turns into rutile VO2(R) above about 68 °C (a thermochromic transition). The card, as the literature uses it, is the monoclinic room-temperature phase, so under v5 D9 the item does not denote a rutile-type oxide. If the review treats a distorted-rutile superstructure as out of scope, this is a clear "no". Full texts of the Wiley, ScienceDirect and Springer papers were read through Frank's existing Purdue EZproxy session in Chrome; no credentials were entered.

C12.caveat: Card 96-210-1931 maps to COD 2101931. That entry is NOT rutile-type. It is the high-pressure CaCl2-type RuO2 (Pnnm, No. 58), refined at 5.3 GPa. The ambient-pressure rutile-type P4_2/mnm entry from the same Haines et al. (1997) paper is COD 2101930 (would be 96-210-1930). The citing paper's 'theoretical (110) spacing 0.315 nm' matches the card: the Pnnm cell of 2101931 gives d(110) = 3.154 A = 0.315 nm, while the rutile cell of 2101930 gives d(110) = 3.177 A = 0.318 nm. So the authors really did use the orthorhombic high-pressure entry as the reference for 'commercial RuO2'. At ambient pressure, commercial RuO2 is almost certainly rutile, and the CaCl2-type is only a slight orthorhombic distortion of rutile (a subgroup), so their powder patterns are almost the same. The card was therefore most likely a mislabelled choice of reference, not evidence of a non-rutile sample. But the item as quoted denotes a Pnnm structure, so it cannot by itself establish the rutile population criterion. A rutile identity for the sample would need other evidence from the paper (for example XRD indexing, or a P4_2/mnm reference such as COD 2101930). The WebSearch budget was used up and DuckDuckGo and Bing were blocked or empty, so the two-independent-papers check could not be done. Seven papers from different groups (2015-2026) tie 44-0141 to alpha-MnO2 (tetragonal, I4/m, hollandite type, 2x2 tunnels). Several also give the card's cell as a = 9.7845 Å and c = 2.8630 Å. COD 9016667 (MnO2, I4/m, a 9.815, c 2.847) and COD 2311065 (Byström 1950, alpha-MnO2, I4/m) confirm that space group. One paper (doi 10.1038/s41598-025-34955-8, PMC12877149) writes 'space group of P42/mnm' for alpha-MnO2 with card 00-44-0141. I judge this a mislabel, not a real disagreement over the phase. That paper names the same phase (alpha-MnO2), and its own peaks rule out a rutile cell: (110) at 12.50° and (200) at 17.97°. Those need a cell of about 9.8 Å. A rutile MnO2 cell (pyrolusite, a 4.398 Å) puts (110) near 28.7°, where alpha-MnO2 has (310). Computed from the card's cell (Cu Ka), the context planes fall at: (110) d = 6.92 Å, 2θ ≈ 12.8°; (310) d = 3.09 Å, 2θ ≈ 28.8°; (211) d = 2.40 Å, 2θ ≈ 37.5°. All three are allowed in I4/m and match alpha-MnO2. One overlap: alpha-MnO2 (211) at about 37.5° lies close to pyrolusite (101) at about 37.3°, so that peak alone does not tell the two apart; the (110) peak at 12.7° does. Paper PMC13119164 cites 'PDF#44-0141' only as 'manganese dioxide' with no polymorph named. The two WebSearch queries were not run because the budget was used up. All evidence comes from the Europe PMC full-text API and COD, which I opened directly. Verdict: the item names a non-rutile (hollandite-type) MnO2 and does not meet the rutile-type population rule.

C14.identity: JCPDS/ICDD PDF card 37-0517 (also 00-037-0517, 037-0517, 37-517) is lead dioxide, PbO2, in its alpha polymorph. That is orthorhombic alpha-PbO2 (scrutinyite type, the synthetic phase), space group Pbcn (No. 60), and it is not a rutile type. Rutile-type beta-PbO2 (plattnerite, tetragonal P4_2/mnm, No. 136) has its own card, 41-1492. In the review record S24686 (Yang et al., Materials 2024), the card is indexed with orthorhombic reflections: (111) 28.5°, (020) 30°, (002) 32.7°, (200) 36°, (221) 50.6° and (113) 55.8°. I computed Cu K-alpha peak positions from the COD 9009091 alpha-PbO2 Pbcn cell: 28.51, 30.01, 32.55, 36.29, 50.75 and 55.63°. These match the paper to within about 0.2°. Rutile beta-PbO2 (COD 9011216 cell) has no reflection at 28.5° or 30°. Its lines fall at 25.39 (110), 31.97 (101), 36.21 (200) and 49.07° (211). So the PbO2 phase in the record, including its '(111)' DFT substrate plane, is alpha-PbO2.

C15.caveat: The ICDD database is closed, so the card itself was not opened. Its identity comes from papers by different groups that quote it, and the space group comes from COD. Most papers read in full (about 30 across groups, years 2013-2026) assign 33-0664 or 00-033-0664 to hematite / alpha-Fe2O3, often calling it rhombohedral with R-3c. Their hkl sets and 2θ values match the COD 9000139 hematite cell. Four isolated papers attach the same number to something else: Fe3O4 (10.1002/advs.202411999), metallic Fe (10.1038/s41598-025-16009-1), recycled expanded polystyrene (10.1016/j.heliyon.2022.e08903), and a 'Cefotax/Cr' complex (10.3390/antibiotics11070967). These look like miscitations: they conflict with the majority and with the hematite hkl/2θ fingerprint. The review rule says to mark a card 'unresolved' when papers attach it to different phases. Here none of the alternative attributions is rutile-type (spinel Fd-3m, bcc Fe, a polymer, a coordination complex), so the rutile-type answer is 'no' under every attribution. The reconciler may still choose to mark it 'unresolved' under a literal reading of the rule. In papers that also contain rutile SnO2, the SnO2 carries a different card (41-1445), so 33-0664 is never used for the rutile phase. Search coverage was partial: the web-search budget was used up, and Europe PMC returned 502/503 errors for many full texts.

C16.identity: Materials Project mp-753512 is TiWO4 (reduced formula O4TiW; cell Ti3W3O12, 18 sites). It is a computed (theoretical) polymorph with no ICSD IDs. MP classifies it as monoclinic, space group P2/m (No. 10), with E_hull = 0.050 eV/atom, so it is not stable. Structurally it is a cation-ordered, symmetry-lowered superstructure derived from rutile. The cell is a = 3.124, b = 4.714, c = 14.18 Å, which is about c_r x a_r x 3a_r of rutile. Ti and W sit on rutile cation sites in the order W/W/Ti/Ti/Ti/W along c, and all six cations are octahedral. When Ti and W are treated as the same species, the framework matches rutile TiO2 (mp-2657, P4_2/mnm). The ordered compound itself is not P4_2/mnm. Esterhuizen et al. (JACS, 10.1021/jacs.3c13491) state that their DFT/Bayesian-optimisation Ir0.5Mo0.5O2 structure is isomorphic to this entry, so that structure is also a P2/m ordered rutile superstructure and not the P4_2/mnm rutile cell.

P18.caveat: Neither In2O3 nor ITO is rutile-type. Every In2O3 polymorph in COD has another space group: I21-3 (Zachariasen's 1927/28 entries), Ia-3 (the bixbyite ground state), R-3c (corundum type) and Pbna (a Rh2O3(II)-type high-pressure phase). The Materials Project OPTIMADE endpoint returns null space-group fields, so the Ia-3 assignment rests on COD 2310009 and 1538147 and on Wikipedia. mp-22598 is only consistent with it: In16O24, a 40-site primitive cell of the 80-atom I-centred cubic cell, sitting on the hull (E_hull 0). One known trap: Meng et al. report that VLS-grown 'indium-tin oxide nanowires' can crystallise as rutile, but they assign that rutile phase to SnO2, not to Sn-doped In2O3. If a paper in the review actually used a Sn-rich In-Sn-O phase or a SnO2 component, that component would need its own check. The Sn-doped In2O3 (ITO) named here is bixbyite. One limitation: the third paper's quote (Zervos et al. 2015) is partly paraphrased by the fetch tool and only its first clause is verbatim, so rely on the other two papers for ITO. The '(111) slab' context fits a cubic bixbyite surface; a (111) surface is also unusual as a termination for tetragonal rutile.

P20.caveat:
In the literature, gamma-MnO2 means one thing: nsutite, the ramsdellite/pyrolusite intergrowth family, with de Wolff disorder and microtwinning. All sources opened agree on this, so the identity is not in conflict. It is not a single ordered phase. So I could not check which bulk cell its authors used to build the slab. A DFT 'gamma-MnO2' slab is normally cut from a ramsdellite-type or ordered-intergrowth cell. If the authors in fact cut a rutile beta-MnO2 cell and called it gamma-MnO2, their model would be rutile-type despite the name. The paper's methods/SI should be checked for the cell and space group before the item is finally excluded.

P21.caveat: The item is not rutile-type. Hollandite shares some motifs with rutile: MO6 octahedra, edge-sharing chains along c with a period of about 3.15 A, and MO2 stoichiometry. But its octahedra form double chains around 2x2 tunnels, and its symmetry is I4/m (87), or I2/m (12) when distorted. It is not P4_2/mnm. By connectivity: in the MP I4/m record each Ir has 4 edge-sharing and 4 corner-sharing Ir neighbours. Kang et al. give rutile as 2 edge-sharing and 8 corner-sharing. Tetragonal and monoclinic settings: most sources give I4/m for K(x)Ir4O8 (Talanov 2014 / COD 4338122; Bertheussen 2024; Kang 2025), and K2Ru8O16 is I4/m (COD 1004080). Quintin-Baxendale 2025, however, assigns their K0.25IrO2 nanowires to I12/m1 and compares them with ICSD 80336. That card was not opened because ICSD is closed; it is probably the Bestaoui 1995 KxIrO2 structure, but I did not verify this. MP also holds a monoclinic C2/m KIr4O8 (mp-30546, 0.0456 eV/atom above hull). Both settings are hollandite, so the rutile verdict is unaffected. 'Hollandite IrO2 (001)' with no K is a computational framework model, not a characterised phase. I found no database entry for K-free hollandite IrO2. Signature warning: the strongest hollandite line near 28 deg 2theta (Cu), (310) with d about 3.18 A from the COD 4338122 cell, nearly coincides with rutile IrO2 (110), d = 3.186 A from COD 2101854. So a single ~28 deg peak cannot tell the phases apart. The hollandite-specific lines are the low-angle (110) at about 12.4 deg (d about 7.1 A) and (200) at about 17.5-17.6 deg (d about 5.0 A), which Quintin-Baxendale and Bertheussen use. Some papers describe mixed hollandite/rutile material (Bertheussen 2024 'rutile/hollandite structure'; Yang 2026 Inorg Chem 'mixture of hollandite- and rutile-type motifs'). A paper can therefore contain a rutile IrO2 comparison phase alongside this item, but the hollandite item itself does not meet the rutile population criterion. P22.caveat:
1) I read "rutile_type = no" under the review's strict population rule (P4_2/mnm, No. 136). WO2 is a rutile-derived structure but has a lower symmetry: monoclinic P2_1/c, Z = 4, the MoO2 type with paired W atoms. Several papers still call it "rutile-type WO2" (for example Ueda et al. 2023, "rutile-type WO2 ... monoclinically distorted rutile structure"). A loose reading of "rutile-type" in a paper should not count as P4_2/mnm. If the review's rule allows distorted rutile derivatives, it has to say so explicitly.
2) Legacy conflict: COD 5910153 gives WO2 as tetragonal P4_2/mnm (a = 4.86 Å, c = 2.77 Å). Its source is Wyckoff's 1931 compilation. The 1995 neutron Rietveld refinement (COD 1548686) replaced this assignment, and the refined structure stays P2_1/c at every tolerance up to 0.5 Å.
3) Computational caveat: the Materials Project ground state mp-19372 is a 6-site cell (a = 3.213, b = 4.805, c = 4.837 Å, gamma = 89.59°) without W–W pairing (all W–W distances 3.213 Å). It is P2_1/c only at tight tolerance and becomes P4_2/mnm at 0.05 Å. A DFT paper that built its "WO2 (011) slab" from mp-19372 or from an ideal rutile model would in practice be using a nearly undistorted rutile model. The paper's own statement of its model structure decides this, and the P22 context does not give it.
4) The Miller index (011) depends on the setting. In the monoclinic P2_1/c cell (Ma et al. 2005 report (011) planes for WO2 nanorods) it is not the same plane as rutile (011), so the index alone does not show which model was used.
5) I could not open the 1979 Palmer and Dickens refinement (the DOI I guessed was wrong, and IUCr returned 403), so the experimental space group rests on the 1995 structure (COD 1548686 and its abstract) plus independent literature statements.
6) I downloaded three temporary files (the OPTIMADE JSON and two COD CIFs) to the session scratchpad to run the symmetry analysis, then deleted them.

S23.identity: These are Raman-active phonons of rutile-type RuO2, ruthenium(IV) oxide. It is tetragonal, space group P4_2/mnm (No. 136), factor group D4h. Rutile RuO2 has four Raman-active modes (B1g, Eg, A1g, B2g), all of which move only oxygen. Eg, A1g and B2g are the three strong modes. In single crystals they sit at 528 (Eg), 646 (A1g; some papers citing the same work give 644) and 716 (B2g) cm-1; this is Huang & Pollak 1982, known here only through papers that cite it. Nanocrystalline RuO2 gives the same three bands shifted lower: about 505-530, 620-647 and 680-716 cm-1. Among the RuO2 polymorphs, this set of mode labels belongs to the rutile phase only. In the high-pressure CaCl2-type phase (Pnnm, No. 58) the Eg mode splits in two. The other high-pressure phase (Pa-3, No. 205) is cubic.

S23.caveat: (1) I could not open the primary source for the single-crystal positions (Huang & Pollak 1982, Solid State Commun. 43, 921). The publisher returned 403 and the abstract is withheld in OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Crossref. The values 528/646/716 cm-1 therefore rest on papers from several different groups that cite it; some of those papers give A1g as 644 instead of 646. (2) The quoted value "A1g near 600 cm-1" is 20-45 cm-1 lower than the single-crystal value (646) and the usual nanocrystalline values (620-647). It falls where other Ru-O phases carrying the same labels have been reported: hydrous RuO2·xH2O at 502/619/682 cm-1 and RuOOH at 482/602/790 cm-1. Some in-situ papers also assign an A1g near 600-610 cm-1. (3) The three-band pattern is not proof of long-range crystalline rutile. Amorphous and hydrous RuO2 show the same Eg/A1g/B2g bands, which authors read as a local rutile RuO6 arrangement. The Raman signature establishes a rutile-type local structure for RuO2, but not crystallinity or phase purity. The Eg ~520 and B2g ~700 values match nanocrystalline rutile RuO2. (4) The labels Eg/A1g/B2g do rule out the other RuO2 polymorphs: the CaCl2-type phase (Pnnm, COD 2101931) splits Eg and appears only above ~11.8 GPa, and the Pa-3 phase is cubic. The same labels are also used for other rutile-type oxides, such as IrO2 at 561/752/728 cm-1, so the band positions are what identify RuO2. (5) The space group for mp-825 is my own spglib result, not a Materials Project field: the OPTIMADE space-group fields are null. The relaxed cell (a = 4.4816, b = 4.4834 Å) gives P4_2/mnm at symprec 0.01 or looser and Pnnm at 0.001. The experimental COD entries 2101930 and 1000058 are P4_2/mnm (136). Verdict: yes. The item denotes rutile-type RuO2, but the quoted A1g position is low and does not by itself exclude hydrous or amorphous RuO2.

S25.caveat: In general, a tetragonal cell (a = 4.505 Å, c = 3.176 Å) does not by itself fix the space group or the atomic arrangement. The rutile type is P4_2/mnm with the metal on 2a and O on 4f (u,u,0), and the quoted item gives no atom positions. The 'yes' rests on combining the cell with the IrO2 composition and the database records. (1) The cell matches the relaxed rutile record mp-2723 to 4 significant figures, and spglib on its coordinates gives P4_2/mnm with O u = 0.3087. (2) No other IrO2 polymorph in the open databases I searched has a similar cell. mp-1014261 is body-centred (conventional cell about 3.925 × 9.78 Å, anatase-like), and mp-1095353 is near-cubic at about 4.90 Å with 12 sites. All 4 COD IrO2 entries are P 42/m n m with a of about 4.49-4.51 Å and c of about 3.14-3.16 Å. (3) The paper builds an IrO2(110) slab from this bulk and compares it with 'rutile oxides' (line 509). The paper itself never says 'rutile' or 'P4_2/mnm' about its bulk cell. Checker 2's 'unresolved' is right about the cell as a bare metric. If the review wants rutile_type decided from the signature alone, with no composition-plus-database match, then it is 'unresolved'. Its experimental comparison values (4.498/3.15 Å, ref [29], unidentified) sit nearest Goldschmidt 1926 (COD 1538153, 4.499/3.146 Å). Trap: c = 3.176 Å is a lattice constant here, but about 3.18-3.19 Å is also the rutile (110) d-spacing (a/√2 = 3.186 Å). Other papers that quote 3.176 Å as a d-spacing, or 4.505 Å for experimental IrO2 or DFT RuO2 (R0080, S15178, S08596), are separate items and should not be merged with this one. The mp-2723 space group comes from my spglib run, because the MP OPTIMADE symmetry fields are null. I did not open the MP web page.

C26.caveat: I did not open the ICDD card itself; the ICDD database is not open. The card's identity rests on seven papers from different groups, and all of them attach 07-0169 to CoOOH. None attaches it to any other phase, so the sources do not conflict. One paper states the space group outright: DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-74386-1 gives 'R-3m'. One more backs the rhombohedral assignment: DOI 10.3389/fchem.2022.855281 says 'hexagonal rhomb-centered'. The (003)/(012)/(015) indexing in DOI 10.1038/s41467-022-30148-3 is the R-3m hexagonal-axis convention, and its peak positions match the COD 9009884 heterogenite-3R cell to within about 0.2 deg 2θ. One paper does not fit. The Mater Today Bio 2025 paper (10.1016/j.mtbio.2025.102018) lists peaks at 23.46, 45.46 and 59.45 deg. These do not match the 3R cell, so that paper's XRD is unreliable, but it still assigns the card to CoOOH. The paper quotes came through the WebFetch summarizer reading Europe PMC full-text XML, so apply the usual caution about how exact they are. The COD CIF was read directly. No open database I reached lists a rutile-type (P4_2/mnm) CoOOH. COD has only the R-3m (3R) and P63/mmc (2H) polytypes. The Materials Project OPTIMADE entries could not be checked for space group through that endpoint. CoOOH as indexed with this card is therefore a layered oxyhydroxide, not a rutile-type oxide.
